1072.title: Body and soul (CCC 362–365)
1072.hook: the soul is the form of the body; together one person
1072.howItsDone: Catholic teaching holds that soul and body form one person, so Catholic worship is bodily: water, oil and bread in the sacraments, and kneeling, standing and the sign of the cross at prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, things visible and invisible: heaven and earth, and the angels. Your line was seen and unseen. Today, where the two meet.

Dust first, then breath. That's the order in the second chapter of Genesis. God shapes the man out of the ground, a figure lying there, finished and still. Then God breathes into him, and only then does he rise. In the Douay-Rheims: "And the Lord God formed man of the slime of the earth: and breathed into his face the breath of life, and man became a living soul." The verse doesn't say God slipped a soul inside a body, the way you'd drop batteries into a flashlight. It says the man became a living soul. The whole of him.

Day one hundred seventy-seven met nephesh in a psalm; today, the Catechism's reading of soul. It begins by refusing to cut a person in half: a human being is at once bodily and spiritual. In scripture, soul often simply means a life, or the whole person. When a psalm says my soul thirsts for God, the whole person is thirsty. But soul can also mean what's innermost in someone, of greatest value, the part by which a person is most especially made in God's image. The Catechism keeps both meanings. Then the body. It shares in the dignity of being made in God's image. It isn't a shell, a costume, or a cage the soul is waiting to escape; it's a human body precisely because a spiritual soul gives it life. Then the sentence the section leans on: the union of soul and body is so deep that the soul is to be considered the form of the body. Form, in this older sense, means roughly what makes a thing the living thing it is. So spirit and matter in a person aren't two natures glued together; their union makes one nature. One person. That has ordinary consequences in Catholic life. The sacraments come through the body: water poured on a forehead, oil on the hands of the sick, bread placed in a palm. Catholics kneel, stand, make the sign of the cross. And the reverse: a tired body shapes a prayer; a grief settles into the shoulders. In this teaching, that isn't a flaw in the design. It is the design.

If you pray, offer the whole of it to God, just as it is; if you don't, stay with the breath, the one Genesis began with.

1073.title: Christ and Lord (CCC 436–451)
1073.hook: Christ means anointed; Lord was the name for God
1073.howItsDone: Catholics name Jesus as Christ and Lord in the Creed at Mass and in the prayers of the liturgy, which often end "through Christ our Lord."

segments.voice: Yesterday, body and soul: dust, then breath, and the soul as the form of the body. Your line was one person. Today, a name that's really a title.

Is Christ a last name? On a form it would look like one. First name, Jesus. Last name, Christ. Easy to hear it that way. But Christ isn't a surname at all. It's a title, a claim about who he is and what he was sent to do. And the word that so often sits beside it, Lord, is a title too, with a history of its own. Today's word is the first of the two.
screen: `NOT A LAST NAME.` → `A TITLE, AND A CLAIM.` → `LORD: A TITLE TOO.`

segments.voice: Day four hundred fifty-one met the Greek word Christos; now, the Catechism's account. Christ comes from the Greek translation of the Hebrew Messiah, and it means anointed. In Israel, those set apart for a mission from God were anointed in his name: kings, priests, and now and then a prophet. Oil poured on the head meant this person now belongs to a task. And the Catechism says Jesus fulfilled all of it, as king, priest and prophet at once. In one scene the title lands. Jesus asks his disciples who people say he is, then asks them directly: "But whom do you say that I am?" Peter answers, in the Douay-Rheims, "Thou art Christ, the Son of the living God." The Catechism adds a careful detail. Jesus accepted the title, but with reserve, because it could easily be heard in a political way, a messiah with an army. He kept turning it toward the cross, toward a Son of Man who came to give his life. Then the second title. In the Greek translation of the Old Testament, God's own holy name, the one not spoken aloud, was rendered Lord, so Lord became an ordinary way of naming God. When the New Testament calls Jesus Lord, it uses that same word. Paul writes that no one can say the Lord Jesus except by the Holy Spirit. And the Catechism draws one more line: a Christian, calling Jesus Lord, refuses to hand absolute power over their freedom to any earthly ruler. Christ: anointed for a mission. Lord: the name once kept for God.

1074.title: Born of the Virgin (CCC 496–507)
1074.hook: the Church professes Jesus was conceived by the Holy Spirit without a human father
1074.howItsDone: Catholics profess the virginal conception in the Creed at Mass, and some pray the Angelus, a short prayer on the Annunciation said traditionally at morning, noon and evening.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Christ and Lord, two titles: anointed, and the name once kept for God. Your line was anointed. Today, how he was born.

A virgin in Nazareth, betrothed to a man named Joseph, has just been told she will have a son, that he will be great, and called the Son of the most High. Luke gives her one question, and it's a practical one. In the Douay-Rheims: "How shall this be done, because I know not man?" She isn't asking for a sign. She's asking how. And the angel's answer is the center of today: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the most High shall overshadow thee." The Apostles' Creed folds that whole scene into a few words: born of the Virgin Mary.
screen: `A VIRGIN IN NAZARETH.` → `HOW SHALL THIS BE DONE?` → `THE HOLY GHOST SHALL COME UPON THEE.`

segments.voice: The Church confesses, the Catechism says, that Jesus was conceived solely by the power of the Holy Spirit in the womb of the Virgin Mary, with no human father. Luke tells it from Mary's side; Matthew from Joseph's. In Matthew, Joseph finds Mary with child and, being a just man, plans to send her away quietly. Then an angel in a dream tells him that what is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost, and he takes her home as his wife. The Catechism is honest that this isn't an easy teaching. People have objected; some have called it a legend. Its reply is not a proof: the Gospels present it as God's own work, beyond human understanding, whose meaning opens up only to faith. What does it mean, in Catholic teaching? First, the beginning is God's: Jesus has only God as his Father. Second, something new is starting: the Catechism calls Jesus the new Adam, the start of a new creation. Third, it's a sign for everyone else, a new birth by the Spirit, which Catholics connect with baptism. Day seventy-nine was the Immaculate Conception; this is a different teaching. The virginal conception is about how Jesus was conceived. The Immaculate Conception is about Mary herself, kept free from original sin from the first moment of her own life. And Mary's last line in Luke's scene is the one the Angelus repeats: "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it done to me according to thy word."
screen: `CONCEIVED BY THE HOLY SPIRIT ALONE.` · `LUKE FROM MARY'S SIDE, MATTHEW JOSEPH'S.` · `GOD'S WORK, OPEN TO FAITH.` · `NOT THE IMMACULATE CONCEPTION.` · then, large: `BE IT DONE TO ME ACCORDING TO THY WORD.`

If you don't, stay with Mary's answer instead, be it done to me according to thy word, and notice how it feels to say yes to something you can't fully see.

1075.title: The hidden life (CCC 531–534)
1075.hook: most of Jesus's life was ordinary work in Nazareth
1075.howItsDone: Catholics honor the hidden life at Nazareth on the feast of the Holy Family and in the rosary's joyful mysteries, which end with the finding of Jesus in the temple.

segments.voice: Yesterday, born of the Virgin: Mary's practical question, and her yes. Your line was by the holy spirit. Today, the years nobody wrote down.

"Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary?" That's the hometown crowd in Mark's Gospel, and they aren't impressed. Jesus has come back to his own country, teaching in the synagogue, and the people who watched him grow up can't square it. They know his mother. They know his brothers by name. They know him as the carpenter. Their question is accidentally a window. Before the crowds and the miracles, there were years so ordinary that the neighbors remembered him mostly as a tradesman. The Catechism has a name for those years.
screen: `IS NOT THIS THE CARPENTER?` → `THE NEIGHBORS CAN'T SQUARE IT.` → `YEARS NOBODY WROTE DOWN.`

segments.voice: The hidden life. For the greater part of his life, the Catechism says, Jesus shared the condition of the vast majority of people: a daily life without evident greatness, manual work, the religious life of his people, life in a community. The Gospels are nearly silent about them. The one event that breaks the silence, the Catechism says, is the finding in the temple. When Jesus was twelve, Luke tells, his family went up to Jerusalem for the feast, and on the way home his parents realized he wasn't with them. After three days they found him in the temple, among the teachers, listening and asking questions. Then a line closes the door on the hidden years again. In the Douay-Rheims: "And he went down with them, and came to Nazareth, and was subject to them." Luke adds one more sentence: "And Jesus advanced in wisdom, and age, and grace with God and men." Back to the workshop, the family table, the synagogue on the sabbath. The Catechism sees in his obedience to Mary and Joseph a picture of his obedience to the Father. And because of Nazareth, it says, anyone can share in Jesus's life through the most ordinary events of their own day. It quotes Pope Paul the Sixth, speaking at Nazareth, who called it a school: a lesson in silence, in family life, in work. So the plain parts of a life aren't a waiting room before the real thing starts. In Catholic teaching, God made flesh spent most of his years on them.

1076.title: Under Pontius Pilate (CCC 595–598)
1076.hook: the Church teaches that Jews are not collectively responsible for his death; all sinners share it
1076.howItsDone: Catholics profess "suffered under Pontius Pilate" in the Creed, and Catholic teaching, following the Second Vatican Council, rejects blaming the Jewish people for the death of Jesus.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the hidden life in Nazareth. Your line was nazareth counts. Today, a governor in the Creed.

In the middle of the Creed, between the words about God and the words about eternity, there's a Roman official. Suffered under Pontius Pilate. A provincial governor, named in a profession of faith. Some readers hear his name as a pin in a map: this happened in a real place, under a real government, at a real time. But his name raises a harder question too, one the Catechism doesn't dodge. Who is responsible for the death of Jesus? Christians have given terrible answers to that question, and the Catechism says so.
screen: `A ROMAN OFFICIAL IN THE CREED.` → `A PIN IN A MAP.` → `WHO IS RESPONSIBLE?`

segments.voice: Day sixty-three stood before Pilate; now, the harder question. The Gospels tell a tangled story: a betrayal by a friend, some of the religious authorities in Jerusalem, a crowd stirred up in the moment, and a governor who finds no cause, washes his hands, and hands Jesus over anyway. Crucifixion was a Roman punishment, and Rome carried it out. The trial's history is complex, the Catechism says, and the personal guilt of each person involved is known to God alone. The responsibility, it says, cannot be laid on the Jews of Jerusalem as a whole. It quotes the Second Vatican Council: what happened in the Passion cannot be charged against all the Jews then living, without distinction, nor against the Jews of today. And Jews are not to be spoken of as rejected or accursed, as if scripture taught it. Then the Catechism turns the question around, quoting the older Roman Catechism: sinners were the authors and ministers of all the sufferings Christ endured. All sinners. So, it says, Christians themselves carry the gravest share, and it admits that Christians have all too often laid that burden on the Jews alone. A confession, written into a book of teaching. At the center is the man on the cross, who in Luke's Gospel prays for the people killing him. In the Douay-Rheims: "Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do." So the Creed's phrase keeps two things together: a real governor in a real province, and a death that, in Catholic teaching, belongs to no single people, because every sinner has a hand in it.

1077.title: He descended (CCC 632–637)
1077.hook: he went to the dead to open heaven for the just who went before
1077.howItsDone: Catholics profess Christ's descent to the dead in the Apostles' Creed, keep Holy Saturday as a quiet day of waiting at the tomb, and pray for the dead, above all at Mass and in November.

segments.voice: Yesterday, under Pontius Pilate: a death charged to no single people. Your line was we all share it. Today, the silent day.

Friday evening, the body is laid in a tomb and a stone is rolled across the door. The women go home and, as Luke puts it, rest on the sabbath according to the commandment. Then Sunday morning, the empty tomb. In between, the Gospels say almost nothing. Catholic churches keep Holy Saturday bare and quiet. And yet the Apostles' Creed has a line for exactly that silence. Between buried and rose again, it says: he descended into hell. It's a strange line to say out loud.
screen: `FRIDAY: THE STONE.` → `SATURDAY: SILENCE.` → `HE DESCENDED INTO HELL.`

segments.voice: Day sixty-seven kept Holy Saturday's quiet; today, the Creed's line for it. First, what hell means there. Scripture, the Catechism says, calls the place of the dead hell: Sheol in Hebrew, Hades in Greek, the realm of those who died before Christ, deprived of the sight of God, the just and the wicked alike, all waiting. So the line isn't saying Jesus went to the place of the damned. The Catechism is precise: he did not go down to free the damned, or to destroy the hell of damnation, but to free the just who had gone before him. Second, it says he truly died: raised from the dead means he had truly been among the dead, as people die. Third, what he did there. The first letter of Peter says that Christ, in the Douay-Rheims, "preached to those spirits that were in prison," and a little later that the gospel was preached even to the dead. The Catechism calls this the last phase of his mission: the good news reaching people of every time and place, all the way back. Then it quotes what it calls an ancient homily for Holy Saturday, where Christ goes down looking for Adam, the first man, like a shepherd looking for a lost sheep, takes him by the hand, and tells him to rise. Some icons of the resurrection paint that moment: Christ standing on broken gates, pulling Adam and Eve up out of their tombs. Holy Saturday looks silent from above. In Catholic teaching, down below it was loud.

1078.title: He will come again (CCC 668–682)
1078.hook: Christ reigns now and will come in glory
1078.howItsDone: Catholics profess at Mass that Christ "will come again in glory to judge the living and the dead," and the season of Advent keeps both his first coming and his return in view.

segments.voice: Yesterday, he descended: Christ among the dead, looking for Adam. Your line was even the dead heard. Today, the coming the Creed waits for.

A group of friends on a hillside outside Jerusalem, heads tipped back, staring at the sky. A cloud has just taken Jesus out of their sight, and they can't stop looking. Then two men in white are standing beside them, and their question is almost funny. In the Douay-Rheims: "Ye men of Galilee, why stand you looking up to heaven? This Jesus who is taken up from you into heaven, shall so come, as you have seen him going into heaven." Stop staring, in other words. He's coming back. Now go.
screen: `HEADS TIPPED BACK.` → `WHY STAND YOU LOOKING UP?` → `HE SHALL SO COME.`

segments.voice: Day seventy-two stood on that hillside; today, the coming it promises. Parousia is the Church's word, from Greek, for Christ's return in glory at the end of time. But the section opens not with the end but with now. Christ already reigns, the Catechism says. Since his ascension he is Lord of the world and of history, and his kingdom is already present, in mystery, in the Church, the seed and beginning of that kingdom on earth. So Catholics live in an in-between: the king already crowned, the kingdom not yet complete. Already, and not yet. And it isn't peaceful. The kingdom is still under attack by evil, the Catechism says, and the Church will pass through a final trial before the end. Then a line that leaves no room for a calendar: the time of his coming is not known. Jesus says no one knows the day or the hour, and in Acts he tells the disciples it is not for them to know the times the Father has set. When he comes, the Creed says, it will be to judge the living and the dead; the Catechism adds that the secrets of hearts will be brought to light. Meanwhile, the Church waits, and the waiting has words. Near the very end of the Bible, Christ's promise gets an answer, in the Douay-Rheims: "Surely I come quickly: Amen. Come, Lord Jesus." Catholics hear the same hope at Mass, just after the Our Father, in a prayer that speaks of awaiting the coming of our Savior.

segments.voice: Look around the day ahead the way a household looks around a room before a guest it loves arrives, not in a panic: a word you'd want to take back, a call you'd want to make, a small mess you'd want set right. Choose just one. If you pray, say the words near the Bible's end, come, Lord Jesus; if you don't, let the guest be anyone you'd be glad to see walk in.
